prompt: A two-week pre-release pen test finds that users of a new invoicing feature can view other customers' invoices. Fixing it means reworking the access model in three services, and the release slips. Which change for the next feature best applies **shifting left**?

options.text: Book a longer pen test just before each release so more issues are found
options.explanation: This keeps the work on the right of the timeline. A longer late test may find more, but every finding still arrives when changing the design is most disruptive.

options.text: Move all security review to a central team that signs off each release
options.explanation: Concentrating review in a late central gate is closer to the opposite of shifting left, which pushes security activities towards design and development.

options.text: Threat-model the design and write abuse cases such as "view another customer's invoice" before coding, then check them in review and tests
options.explanation: Correct. Shifting left moves security work earlier: an authorisation flaw found in the design or a pull request is fixed while the context is fresh and before other services depend on it. The pre-release test still has value as a later check.

options.text: Ship on time and schedule access-control fixes for a later sprint
options.explanation: Deferral moves work later and leaves the exposure live in the meantime; it does not move any security activity earlier.

workedExample:
1. Ask where the flaw was introduced: in the design of the access model, before any code was written.
2. Ask where it was found: in a pen test just before release, after three services had been built around that design.
3. Shifting left means adding a security activity at the point of introduction, here design-time threat modelling and an attacker-side abuse case, plus checks on each pull request.
4. Keep the later pen test and monitoring: earlier checks complement them. How much rework this saves depends on the defect and project; no fixed cost multiplier is implied.

link.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

prompt: An engineering director wants to know whether the organisation's secure-development practices are improving year on year, across 30 teams, against a recognised framework. What fits best?

options.text: Count the number of SAST findings each year; fewer means better
options.explanation: Raw finding counts are easily gamed (disable rules, scan less code) and say nothing about design review, incident response or training.

options.text: Run an annual external pen test and compare the number of high-severity findings
options.explanation: A pen test samples one application at one point in time. It measures outcomes for that target, not the maturity of practices across 30 teams.

options.text: Assess each team against a maturity model such as OWASP SAMM (or map practices to NIST SSDF) and track the scores over time
options.explanation: Correct. SAMM defines practices across governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, each with maturity levels, so you can measure where teams are and set targets.

options.text: Adopt OWASP ASVS Level 3 for every application
options.explanation: ASVS is a list of verification requirements for an *application*, not a model for measuring the maturity of an organisation's *process*. Level 3 everywhere would also be excessive for most apps.

workedExample:
1. The question is about *process maturity across an organisation*, not the security of one app.
2. SAMM is built for this: business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), each split into practices with maturity levels 1 to 3.
3. Teams self-assess or are assessed; the scores give a baseline and a roadmap.
4. NIST SSDF lists practices you can map against, useful for US government suppliers.
5. ASVS answers 'is this application verified to level N?', which is complementary but different.
